request.input: So, based on what you told me, I should ask my dad what kind of birthday celebration he'd prefer. Is that correct?

content.text:
Actually, **no—I would recommend against that.**

If your dad is as humble as you described, asking him "what he wants" or "how he wants to celebrate" will almost certainly result in him saying: *"Oh, I don't need anything," "Just a quiet dinner is fine,"* or *"Don't spend your money on me."*

Humble people often feel a sense of burden when they have to "request" something or "choose" a gift. It makes them feel like they are being demanding.

**Instead of asking him what he wants, tell him what you have planned.**

There is a big difference between **asking for permission** and **making an invitation.**

*   **Asking (Low success rate):** "What would you like to do for your birthday? Would you want to go to a game?" $\rightarrow$ *He will likely say no to save you money.*
*   **Inviting (High success rate):** "Dad, I've really wanted to see a hockey game and I want you to be the one to take me. I've got it all figured out, I just need you to come with me next week." $\rightarrow$ *He is now doing you a favor by coming along.*

**The Strategy:**
Since you already know he loves hockey and you already know you want to take him, **take the lead.** 

If you want to give him a little heads-up without giving him a chance to talk you out of it, you can say:
*"Dad, I know your birthday was last week and I didn't do anything big, so I'm planning a little surprise for us next week. Keep [Day of the Week] open, okay?"*

By framing it as a **plan** rather than a **question**, you remove the "guilt" he feels about the cost and replace it with the excitement of spending time with you.
